PSE II · Chapter 31

Electromagnetic Waves

Light as a field phenomenon

← PSE II Course

31.0 — What Light Is Made Of

Chapter 30 treated light as a wave without saying what is waving. Interference and diffraction need something with an amplitude that adds and cancels, and Young’s fringes measured its wavelength, but the optics of 1830 had no candidate for what that something was. The answer came out of electricity and magnetism.

In the early 1860s James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) wrote the known laws of electric and magnetic fields as a single set, found that one of them was incomplete, and added a term to fix it. With that term in place the laws allow a disturbance of electric and magnetic fields to travel through empty space on its own, at a speed fixed by two constants measured on a lab bench with charges, currents and capacitors. The speed came out at about \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s, the measured speed of light.

“We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.” — James Clerk Maxwell, “On Physical Lines of Force,” Part III, Philosophical Magazine (1862)

Maxwell’s full statement, “A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field” (1865), did not look like the four laws in this chapter. He wrote the theory component by component, about twenty equations in twenty unknowns, several of them in terms of potentials rather than the fields. In 1884–1885 Oliver Heaviside (1850–1925), a self-taught telegraph engineer, rewrote the theory in the vector notation he had developed for his own work and reduced it to four equations in \(\vec E\) and \(\vec B\), published in the journal The Electrician. J. Willard Gibbs at Yale developed a nearly identical vector notation independently, and Heinrich Hertz arrived at the same compact form; for a time the four were called the Hertz–Heaviside equations. The “Maxwell’s equations” on every physics poster are Heaviside’s form of Maxwell’s theory.

*Sources: Maxwell, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 155, 459 (1865); Heaviside, “Electromagnetic Induction and its Propagation,” The Electrician (1885–1887), collected in his Electrical Papers (1892); B. J. Hunt, The Maxwellians (Cornell, 1991).

Maxwell still pictured a medium. The modern statement drops it: the fields themselves are the wave, and they need nothing to travel through. In 1887–1888 Heinrich Hertz (1857–1894) built a spark circuit that radiated these waves and a separate loop that detected them across his laboratory, then measured their wavelength and showed that they travel at the speed of light. The unit of frequency carries his name.

*A note on order: in this course Chapter 31 comes before Chapters 28 and 29, which treat magnetism. This chapter uses only two facts about the magnetic field that those chapters develop, and it names them where they appear. Everything it derives rests on flux (Chapter 23) and the capacitor (Chapter 25).

31.1 — Four Field Laws

A Second Field

Chapters 22–27 needed one field, \(\vec E\), produced by charges. There is a second, the magnetic field \(\vec B\), produced by moving charges — currents and magnets. Its SI unit is the tesla (T). Earth’s magnetic field at the surface is about \(50\ \mu\text{T}\); a refrigerator magnet is around \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) T near its face. Chapter 28 gives the force \(\vec B\) exerts and the fields that currents make. This chapter needs only two facts: \(\vec B\) is a vector field like \(\vec E\), and it has a flux.

Flux and Circulation

Two measurements of a vector field run through all four laws (Figure 31.1).

Flux through a surface (Chapter 23): split the surface into small patches \(d\vec A\), each pointing along the patch’s normal, and add up the component of the field through each:

\[\Phi_E = \int \vec E \cdot d\vec A, \qquad \Phi_B = \int \vec B \cdot d\vec A\]

\(\Phi_B\) is defined exactly as \(\Phi_E\) was; its unit is \(\text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2\), also called the weber (Wb). For a uniform field perpendicular to a flat area \(A\), \(\Phi_B = BA\).

Circulation around a closed loop: split the loop into small steps \(d\vec\ell\) and add up the component of the field along each step, \(\oint \vec E \cdot d\vec\ell\). Chapter 24 met this sum without the name: for the field of static charges, \(\int \vec E \cdot d\vec\ell\) between two points is \(-\Delta V\) and does not depend on the path, so around any closed loop it is zero. The direction a loop is traversed and the normal of the surface it bounds are tied together by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along the traversal, and the thumb gives the normal.

The Four Laws

Each law sets either a flux out of a closed surface or a circulation around a loop. The integral form states it for a surface or loop of any size. The vector form states the same law at a single point, by shrinking the surface or loop down to nothing:

  • Divergence, \(\nabla\cdot\vec E\): the flux out of a tiny closed surface, divided by the volume it encloses. “Flux out per unit volume.”
  • Curl, \(\nabla\times\vec E\): its component along a direction \(\hat n\) is the circulation around a tiny loop with normal \(\hat n\), divided by the loop’s area. “Circulation per unit area.”

The charge and current then appear per unit volume and per unit area: \(\rho\) is the charge density (C/m³) and \(\vec J\) the current density (A/m²).

Law Integral form Vector form In words
(1) Gauss \(\oint \vec E \cdot d\vec A = \dfrac{Q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\nabla\cdot\vec E = \dfrac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}\) Electric flux out of a closed surface counts the charge inside.
(2) Gauss, magnetic \(\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec A = 0\) \(\nabla\cdot\vec B = 0\) No magnetic charge: \(\vec B\) lines close on themselves.
(3) Faraday \(\oint \vec E \cdot d\vec\ell = -\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\) \(\nabla\times\vec E = -\dfrac{\partial\vec B}{\partial t}\) A changing magnetic flux makes a circulating \(\vec E\).
(4) Ampère–Maxwell \(\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0 I_\text{enc} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\) \(\nabla\times\vec B = \mu_0\vec J + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\dfrac{\partial\vec E}{\partial t}\) A current, or a changing electric flux, makes a circulating \(\vec B\).

*The vector form is here so you can read it when you meet it in later courses; this course and its exams work with the integral form only.

Law (1) is yours from Chapter 23. Law (3) contains the static result of Chapter 24 as the special case of a magnetic flux that is not changing; the circulation of \(\vec E\) around a circuit is the EMF of Chapter 26, so Faraday’s law says a changing magnetic flux drives a current with no battery, which is how every generator works. In law (4), \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) is the permeability of free space, the magnetic counterpart of \(\varepsilon_0\). Its first term alone is Ampère’s law; the second is Maxwell’s addition, which §31.2 derives. *Laws (2)–(4) are stated here; Chapters 28 and 29 develop them.

The fourth column holds the point of the chapter. A changing \(\vec B\) makes an \(\vec E\), and a changing \(\vec E\) makes a \(\vec B\). Each field can keep the other going with no charge or current anywhere nearby.

31.2 — The Displacement Current

Ampère’s law without Maxwell’s term, \(\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}\), counts the current through any surface bounded by the loop. A charging capacitor shows that “any” fails.

A current \(I_C\) (the conduction current, carried by moving charge) charges the plates. Through the flat surface \(S_1\) the wire carries \(I_C\); through the bag \(S_2\), which passes between the plates, no charge crosses. One loop, two answers. But between the plates the charge is piling up, so the electric field there is growing, and its flux is something only flux can account for.

Step 1 — the flux through \(S_2\). Plates of area \(A\) with charge \(\pm Q\) have a uniform field \(E = Q/(\varepsilon_0 A)\) between them (Chapter 25), and all of it passes through \(S_2\):

\[\Phi_E = EA = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\]

Step 2 — its rate of change is the wire’s current. \(dQ/dt\) is the current arriving on the plate:

\[\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{I_C}{\varepsilon_0}\]

Step 3 — multiply by \(\varepsilon_0\). The result has the units of a current and the value of the wire’s current. It is the displacement current:

\[\boxed{\;I_d = \varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = I_C\;}\]

Counting \(I_d\) in Ampère’s law gives \(\mu_0 I_C\) through either surface, which is law (4). \(I_d\) is not a flow of charge; no charge crosses the gap, and the name is historical. What the result says is that the magnetic field cannot tell the difference between charge flowing and electric flux changing at the matching rate.

Check the result.

  • A fully charged capacitor. \(Q\) is constant, so \(\Phi_E\) is constant and \(I_d = 0\), matching \(I_C = 0\).
  • Units. \(\varepsilon_0\,\Phi_E/t\): \(\frac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\cdot\frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{C}}\cdot\frac{1}{\text{s}} = \frac{\text{C}}{\text{s}} = \text{A}\).
  • Continuity. Chapter 26 required current to be continuous around a circuit. Counting \(I_d\), it is: \(I_C\) in the wire, \(I_d\) in the gap, \(I_C\) again in the other wire.

*Personal note: Maxwell added this term before any experiment demanded it. Currents into capacitors were small and slow in the 1860s, and the magnetic field in the gap was far too weak to measure. The term earned its place a quarter century later, when Hertz detected the waves it predicts.

31.3 — A Wave from the Field Laws

The last column of the table in §31.1 suggests a loop that needs no charges at all. A changing \(\vec E\) makes a \(\vec B\) (law 4). If that \(\vec B\) is itself changing, it makes an \(\vec E\) (law 3), which changes and makes a \(\vec B\), and so on. A disturbance of the two fields can therefore carry itself through empty space. Applying laws (3) and (4) to a front of field moving into empty space fixes three things about it:

\[\boxed{\;c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}, \qquad E = cB, \qquad \text{travel along } \vec E \times \vec B\;}\]

*The derivation takes one loop for each of laws (3) and (4), straddling the moving front; it is stated here and comes within reach after Chapter 29.

With the measured constants,

\[c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(8.854\times10^{-12})}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.1127\times10^{-17}}} = 2.998\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}\]

No optics went into this number. \(\varepsilon_0\) comes from the force between charges (Coulomb’s law, Chapter 22) and \(\mu_0\) from the force between currents. That the result equals the measured speed of light is the evidence that light is an electromagnetic wave.

Check the result.

  • Units. \(\mu_0\varepsilon_0\) has units \(\frac{\text{T}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{A}}\cdot\frac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\). With \(\text{T} = \text{N}/(\text{A}\cdot\text{m})\) (Chapter 28) and \(\text{C} = \text{A}\cdot\text{s}\), this is \(\text{s}^2/\text{m}^2\), so \(1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\) is a speed.
  • Neither field alone. With \(B = 0\), law (3) leaves nothing to make the changing \(\vec E\), and \(E = cB\) gives \(E = 0\). The wave exists only as a pair.
  • Size of \(B\). \(B = E/c\). A field of \(E = 300\) V/m comes with \(B = 1.0\ \mu\text{T}\), a fiftieth of Earth’s field. In SI units the magnetic half of a light wave is always the small-looking one, though §31.5 shows it carries exactly half the energy.

31.4 — Sinusoidal Electromagnetic Waves

The Wave Functions

What sets the pattern is the source. A charge that oscillates at frequency \(f\) — the electrons in an antenna, driven by an AC current — sends out fields that oscillate at the same \(f\). *That accelerating charges radiate is a result of the field laws that this course does not derive. Far from the source the wave is, to a very good approximation, a plane wave: for travel in \(+x\) with \(\vec E\) along \(y\),

\[E_y(x,t) = E_0 \sin(kx - \omega t), \qquad B_z(x,t) = B_0 \sin(kx - \omega t)\]

\(k = 2\pi/\lambda\) and \(\omega = 2\pi f\) are the wavenumber and angular frequency of PSE-I Ch 16, and \(E_0\), \(B_0\) are the amplitudes. The pattern moves at \(\omega/k = f\lambda\), which §31.3 fixed:

\[\boxed{\;c = f\lambda, \qquad E_0 = cB_0\;}\]

Because \(E = cB\) at every point and instant, the two fields are in phase: they reach their maxima and pass through zero together. The wave is transverse: both fields are perpendicular to the direction of travel. And at every point \(\vec E \times \vec B\) points along \(+x\): when \(E_y\) goes negative, \(B_z\) goes negative with it, and \((-\hat y)\times(-\hat z) = +\hat x\).

The direction along which \(\vec E\) oscillates is the wave’s polarization. The wave above is polarized along \(y\). Sunlight and lamplight are mixtures of all polarization directions; a polarizing filter passes one.

In a Transparent Material

Chapter 30 described light in glass or water by the index \(n\): the speed drops to \(v = c/n\), the frequency stays the source’s, and the wavelength shrinks to \(\lambda_n = \lambda/n\) (§30.6). The field picture describes what the material’s charges are doing.

The wave’s \(\vec E\) pushes the electrons in the glass back and forth. They are driven oscillators (PSE-I §15.6): once a driven oscillator settles, it moves at the driving frequency, not at a frequency of its own. So the electrons oscillate at \(f\), and like the electrons in an antenna they radiate at \(f\). The wave inside the material is the incoming wave plus the waves those electrons send out, all at \(f\). The frequency is set by the source; the speed is set by the material. *That this sum travels more slowly than \(c\) is stated here, not derived. Writing \(v = f\lambda\) on each side, \(c = f\lambda\) in vacuum and \(c/n = f\lambda_n\) in the material, and dividing:

\[\boxed{\;f_\text{material} = f, \qquad v = \frac{c}{n}, \qquad \lambda_n = \frac{\lambda}{n}\;}\]

Written as \(\lambda_n = v \cdot \frac{1}{f}\), the result has the same shape as Ohm’s law written as \(I = V/R\). A behavior is the product of an intrinsic response and an extrinsic drive. In Ohm’s law the resistor’s conductance \(1/R\) is intrinsic, the potential difference \(V\) across it is imposed from outside, and the current is what results. Here the material’s speed \(v\) is intrinsic, the source’s period \(1/f\) is imposed from outside, and the wavelength is what results: the distance the material lets the wave travel in one period of the source. The product form also has a limit. A shorter wavelength, seen on its own, cannot say whether the source sped up or the material slowed the wave down. It takes a second measurement, the frequency, to separate the two.

Check the result.

  • Vacuum. At \(n = 1\), \(v = c\) and \(\lambda_n = \lambda\): nothing changes.
  • Color. The eye responds to the frequency. Red helium–neon light, \(\lambda = 633\) nm, has \(\lambda_n = 633/1.33 = 476\) nm in water, which is a blue vacuum wavelength. It is still \(4.74 \times 10^{14}\) Hz, so it still looks red underwater.

Example: An FM Broadcast

An FM station broadcasts at \(f = 98.7\) MHz. At a car’s antenna the electric field amplitude is \(E_0 = 0.0500\) V/m. Find the wavelength and the magnetic field amplitude.

Step 1 — the wavelength.

\[\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3.00\times10^8}{98.7\times10^6} = 3.04\ \text{m}\]

Step 2 — the magnetic amplitude.

\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{0.0500}{3.00\times10^8} = 1.67\times10^{-10}\ \text{T}\]

\[\boxed{\;\lambda = 3.04\ \text{m}, \qquad B_0 = 1.67\times10^{-10}\ \text{T}\;}\]

Plausibility. A common car whip antenna is about 0.75 m long, a quarter of this wavelength, which is the length at which a simple antenna responds best. A \(B_0\) of \(10^{-10}\) T is a few millionths of Earth’s field; the receiver works because it responds to the oscillation at 98.7 MHz, not to the size of the field.

31.5 — Energy and Intensity

Equal Shares

A wave carries energy: sunlight warms what it lands on. The energy is stored in the fields. Chapter 25 found the energy density of an electric field, \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2\). A magnetic field stores energy with density \(u_B = B^2/2\mu_0\) (*derived in Chapter 29 from the energy in an inductor; used here as stated). Substitute \(B = E/c\) and \(\mu_0 = 1/(\varepsilon_0c^2)\), the second from squaring \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\):

\[u_B = \frac{(E/c)^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{E^2\,\varepsilon_0 c^2}{2c^2} = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2 = u_E\]

The energy is shared equally between the two fields at every point and instant, and the total is \(u = u_E + u_B = \varepsilon_0E^2\).

The Poynting Vector

Step 1 — energy carried across an area. Take an area \(A\) perpendicular to the direction of travel (Figure 31.4). In a time \(dt\) the wave moves \(c\,dt\), so all the energy in the box of volume \(A\,c\,dt\) behind the area crosses it:

\[dU = u\,A\,c\,dt\]

Step 2 — per unit time, per unit area. Divide by \(A\,dt\), then replace one factor of \(E\) by \(cB\) and use \(c^2\varepsilon_0 = 1/\mu_0\):

\[S = \frac{dU}{A\,dt} = c\varepsilon_0E^2 = c\varepsilon_0E(cB) = \frac{EB}{\mu_0}\]

\(\vec E\) and \(\vec B\) are perpendicular, so \(EB\) is the magnitude of \(\vec E\times\vec B\), which points along the travel. One vector holds both the rate and the direction of energy flow, the Poynting vector (J. H. Poynting, 1884), in \(\text{W/m}^2\):

\[\boxed{\;\vec S = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\,\vec E\times\vec B\;}\]

Intensity: the Average

Step 3 — average over a cycle. In a sinusoidal wave \(E^2 = E_0^2\sin^2(kx - \omega t)\), which swings between \(0\) and \(E_0^2\) about \(10^{14}\) times a second for visible light. Any detector, from an eye to a solar cell, responds to the average. \(\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1\) at every instant, and over a full cycle the two take the same values, one shifted a quarter period from the other (Figure 31.5), so each averages to \(\tfrac12\). The intensity is the average of \(S\):

\[\boxed{\;I = S_\text{avg} = \tfrac12 c\varepsilon_0E_0^2 = \frac{E_0B_0}{2\mu_0}\;}\]

(\(I\) is intensity here, as in Chapter 30, not current.)

Step 4 — intensity from a power. A beam of power \(P\) spread evenly over a cross-section \(A\) has \(I = P/A\). A source that radiates power \(P\) equally in all directions spreads it over a sphere of area \(4\pi r^2\) (Figure 31.6):

\[\boxed{\;I = \frac{P}{A}, \qquad I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}\ \text{(equal in all directions)}\;}\]

Check the result.

  • Units. \(c\varepsilon_0E^2\): \(\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\cdot\frac{\text{C}^2}{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}\cdot\frac{\text{N}^2}{\text{C}^2} = \frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{s}\cdot\text{m}^2} = \frac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}\).
  • Amplitude squared. Doubling \(E_0\) quadruples \(I\), as for every wave in PSE-I Ch 16. Chapter 30’s \(I = I_0\cos^2(\delta/2)\) for two slits is this rule applied to the electric field.
  • Inverse square. \(P/4\pi r^2\) falls as \(1/r^2\), the geometry of Coulomb’s law (Chapter 22): the same power through ever larger spheres.

Example: Sunlight

Above the atmosphere, sunlight arrives with intensity \(I = 1.36\ \text{kW/m}^2\) (the solar constant). Find \(E_0\) and \(B_0\), and the Sun’s total power. Earth is \(r = 1.50 \times 10^{11}\) m from the Sun.

Step 1 — the electric amplitude.

\[E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(1360)}{(3.00\times10^8)(8.854\times10^{-12})}} = 1.01\times10^3\ \text{V/m}\]

Step 2 — the magnetic amplitude.

\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = 3.37\times10^{-6}\ \text{T} = 3.37\ \mu\text{T}\]

Step 3 — the Sun’s power. The Sun radiates equally in all directions, so

\[P = I\cdot4\pi r^2 = (1360)(4\pi)(1.50\times10^{11})^2 = 3.85\times10^{26}\ \text{W}\]

\[\boxed{\;E_0 = 1.01\ \text{kV/m}, \quad B_0 = 3.37\ \mu\text{T}, \quad P_\text{Sun} = 3.85\times10^{26}\ \text{W}\;}\]

Plausibility. The electric field of full sunlight is about a three-thousandth of the field that breaks down air (\(3 \times 10^6\) V/m), which is why sunlight does not make sparks. And the power, found from a measurement made at Earth, matches the Sun’s output found by other routes (its surface temperature and size).

31.6 — The Electromagnetic Spectrum

Nothing in §31.3–31.5 fixed the frequency. The field laws allow electromagnetic waves at any frequency, all travelling at \(c\) in vacuum with \(c = f\lambda\). Visible light is the narrow band that human eyes respond to.

Region Frequency Wavelength Sources and uses
Radio below 300 MHz above 1 m broadcasting, MRI
Microwave 300 MHz – 300 GHz 1 mm – 1 m radar, Wi-Fi, phones, ovens
Infrared 300 GHz – 400 THz 750 nm – 1 mm warm objects, remote controls
Visible 400 – 750 THz 400 – 750 nm the Sun, lamps; vision
Ultraviolet 750 THz – 30 PHz 10 – 400 nm the Sun; sterilization
X-ray 30 PHz – 30 EHz 0.01 – 10 nm medical imaging, crystallography
Gamma ray above 30 EHz below 0.01 nm nuclear decay

The boundaries are conventions; nothing physical changes at them. Within the visible band, red is the long-wavelength end (about 700 nm, 430 THz) and violet the short (about 400 nm, 750 THz).

Photon Energy

Section 30.0 noted that light also delivers its energy in packets, photons. Each photon of frequency \(f\) carries energy

\[E_\text{ph} = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\]

where \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}\) is Planck’s constant. (The subscript keeps photon energy apart from the field \(E\).) The wave picture fixes how much energy a beam carries; the photon picture fixes how it is divided up. *Where \(E_\text{ph} = hf\) comes from is quantum physics, beyond this course; it is used here only to compare regions of the spectrum.

Example: Why Microwaves Heat and Ultraviolet Burns

Compare the photon energy of a microwave oven (\(f = 2.45\) GHz) with that of green light (\(\lambda = 530\) nm), in electron-volts (\(1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}\) J, Chapter 24).

\[E_\text{microwave} = hf = (6.626\times10^{-34})(2.45\times10^9) = 1.62\times10^{-24}\ \text{J} = 1.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{eV}\]

\[E_\text{green} = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^8)}{530\times10^{-9}} = 3.75\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 2.3\ \text{eV}\]

Chemical bonds hold with a few electron-volts. A green photon is close to that scale, which is why light can drive chemistry (in the eye and in leaves), and ultraviolet photons, at several eV, can break bonds in skin. A microwave photon is more than 200,000 times too small to break anything; microwaves heat food by making water molecules swing back and forth, not by breaking them.

*Personal note: the visible band spans less than one octave — red to violet is a factor of about 1.8 in frequency. Human hearing spans about ten octaves, 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Almost all of the electromagnetic world is invisible to us, and nearly everything we know about it beyond that sliver came from instruments.

31.7 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Two fields, four laws. Gauss’s laws fix the flux of \(\vec E\) and \(\vec B\) out of closed surfaces; Faraday’s law and the Ampère–Maxwell law fix their circulation around loops. Heaviside wrote Maxwell’s twenty equations as these four, in integral and vector form.
  2. Displacement current. A charging capacitor gives Ampère’s law two answers unless the changing electric flux counts as a current: \(I_d = \varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt = I_C\). No charge crosses the gap.
  3. The wave. A changing \(\vec E\) makes \(\vec B\) and a changing \(\vec B\) makes \(\vec E\), so the pair travels through empty space at \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3.00\times10^8\) m/s, with \(E = cB\) and travel along \(\vec E\times\vec B\).
  4. Sinusoidal waves. \(E\) and \(B\) oscillate in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the travel; \(c = f\lambda\), \(E_0 = cB_0\). In a material the driven electrons keep the source’s \(f\); \(v = c/n\) and \(\lambda_n = \lambda/n\).
  5. Energy. \(u_E = u_B\), so \(u = \varepsilon_0E^2\); \(\vec S = \vec E\times\vec B/\mu_0\); intensity \(I = \tfrac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2\), with \(I = P/A\) for a beam and \(I = P/4\pi r^2\) for a source radiating equally.
  6. The spectrum. Radio through gamma rays are one phenomenon at different frequencies; \(E_\text{ph} = hf\) sets what each region can do to matter.

Looking Ahead

This chapter used \(\vec B\) mostly as the partner that keeps \(\vec E\) moving. Chapter 28 takes the magnetic field on its own terms: the force it exerts on a moving charge and on a current, and the fields that currents produce, which is the static half of the Ampère–Maxwell law. Chapter 29 then supplies Faraday’s law from experiment and sets all four laws side by side again, with every piece resting on a chapter of its own.
